title: Meter Prover Guide: 5 Essential Types for Confident Proving
text:
Flow

 Meter Prover Guide: 5 Essential Types for Confident Proving

 Every litre of crude, diesel or LPG sold through a pipeline is billed from a flow meter reading, so a tiny meter error becomes a large money error. Proving that meter against a known volume, under real flowing conditions, keeps both buyer and seller confident.

 
 Pipe and Ball Provers 
 Compact Prover 
 Master Meter 
 Meter Factor 
 API MPMS Chapter 4 
 




 A custody transfer flow meter is only as trustworthy as its last proving run. This guide explains how each prover type works, how the meter factor is calculated and how to judge repeatability in the field.


 
 Hello everyone, today we are going to learn how a meter prover works, the five main prover types, how API MPMS Chapter 4 defines proving, and how to calculate a meter factor with correction factors.


 
 
 
 What Is a Meter Prover?


 A meter prover is a device with an accurately known reference volume that is used to check a flow meter in service, under actual flowing conditions of product, pressure and temperature. It is the backbone of custody transfer measurement for crude oil, refined products and LPG.


 During a proving run, liquid flows through the flow meter and then through the prover in series. The flow computer compares the volume the meter indicated with the certified volume the prover displaced, and the ratio becomes the meter factor.


 
 
 Image credit: Flow Management Devices . Photo courtesy of Flow Management Devices, shown here for educational reference. 
 

 Unlike a laboratory calibration, a meter prover checks the meter in its own piping with the real product. Viscosity, temperature and installation effects are therefore included in the result.


 Do You Know?
 The American Petroleum Institute publishes the Manual of Petroleum Measurement Standards, and Chapter 4 is entirely about proving systems. Its sections cover displacement provers, tank provers, master meters, pulse interpolation, operation and waterdraw calibration.



 
 
 Advertisement 


 
 


 How a Displacement Meter Prover Measures Volume


 A displacement meter prover is a calibrated length of pipe with a sphere or piston that moves with the flow. Two detector switches mark the start and end of a precisely known section, and the volume between them is called the base volume.


 
 Divert Flow Four way valve or piston launch sends product into the prover

 First Detector Displacer trips switch one, flow computer starts counting meter pulses

 Calibrated Section Displacer sweeps the known base volume

 Second Detector Switch two stops the pulse count

 Calculate Flow computer applies corrections and computes the meter factor




 The meter sends pulses in proportion to volume, as explained in flow meter K factor calculations . The flow computer divides the pulse count by the K factor to get the indicated volume and compares it with the corrected prover volume.


 Greg Williams notes in his ASGMT paper on meter provers that a conventional pipe meter prover must collect at least 10,000 whole meter pulses in a single pass. The same paper gives a sphere velocity window of about 1 to 5 feet per second for a unidirectional pipe prover.


 5 Essential Meter Prover Types


 
 Unidirectional Pipe Prover
 A sphere travels one way through a loop and is returned to the launch chamber.
 Best for: large pipeline and terminal meters
 Classic 

 Bidirectional Ball Prover
 A four way valve drives a sphere forward and back, one round trip per run.
 Best for: fixed custody skids
 Common 

 Compact or Small Volume Prover
 A precision piston in a short honed cylinder sweeps a small volume and uses pulse interpolation.
 Best for: skids with limited space, mobile units
 Compact 

 Master Meter
 A proved reference meter placed in series with the meter under test.
 Best for: high flow or viscous products
 Indirect 

 Tank Prover
 An open or closed certified volumetric tank receives a batch of product from the meter.
 Best for: loading racks and low flow meters
 Simple 




 Williams defines a small volume meter prover as a displacement prover that does not have enough reference volume to accumulate 10,000 pulses in one pass. It therefore relies on pulse interpolation to resolve fractions of a pulse.


 A master meter is usually a Coriolis flow meter or a turbine meter that is itself proved on a displacement prover. The ASGMT paper recommends that the master be roughly ten times more accurate than the meter under test.


 Quick Tip
 Before a proving campaign, confirm that the meter prover base volume certificate is still valid and that its serial number matches the nameplate. An expired waterdraw certificate makes every meter factor from that prover disputable.



 Meter Prover and Meter Factor Formula


 The meter factor from a meter prover corrects the meter so that its reading matches true volume at base conditions. Both the prover volume and the meter volume must first be corrected for temperature and pressure effects on the steel and on the liquid.


 
 Meter factor MF = Corrected prover volume ÷ Corrected meter volume 
 Prover volume = Base volume × CTSp × CPSp × CTLp × CPLp 
 Meter volume = (Pulses ÷ K factor) × CTLm × CPLm 

Example:
Base volume 1000 L, combined prover corrections 0.9985
Meter pulses 50,120 at K factor 50 pulses per L
Indicated volume = 50,120 ÷ 50 = 1002.4 L
Combined meter corrections 0.9990, so meter volume = 1001.40 L
Prover volume = 1000 × 0.9985 = 998.5 L
 MF = 998.5 ÷ 1001.40 = 0.9971, meter reads high by 0.29 percent 



 CTSp and CPSp correct the steel prover for thermal expansion and pressure stretch, while CTL and CPL correct the liquid itself. These are the same ideas used in temperature and pressure compensation of flow signals.
